title: Tricky Sam gets his solo and the growl of 'Black and Tan Fantasy'
summary: Duke ignored Tricky Sam Nanton until Otto Hardwick insisted; the growl duets with Bubber Miley came from the men and Duke wrote 'Black and Tan Fantasy' for them.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: That's the way it was, you see. See, like when -- they told me when Tricky Sam first came in his band -- he took a guy's, name I think it was Charlie Irvin or

He took his place and that's when he had six piece group. And Tricky hadn't taken a solo at all at no time, see. But when the band augmented in the Cotton Club, and one night Duke was telling everybody to take solo but Tricky. Tricky was sitting there with his horn on his lap and his plunger in his hand and Otto Hardwick looked at Duke, he says, "Duke, damn it, why don't you let that man take a solo? Don't you see he's dying to play it and you haven't given him one?"

So Duke finally told him to take one and he fell madly in love with Tricky because Tricky -- it was like a tradition of the band. He and Bubber Miley, you see, they made duets together, like in "Black and Tan Fantasy" and things like that, where they would growl on the horn like that. That was like an identification of Ellington's band.
Where did that -- did that evolve from the men or was that something that Duke arranged or what in "Black and Tan Fantasy"?
Oh, that's from the men themselves.
But Duke wrote the tune for that purpose, for them to growl that tune, you see, --
-- and that's how the "Black and Tan Fantasy" came on. And every time Tricky took a solo and he was growling or whatever it was, like -- I don't know whether you ever heard the record of "Chloë."
It's like he's talking to you, you know, he's growling at you, you know. It's just like he's talking to you, and that's what he wanted.
